claims.text: The target material is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr in the cast state.
Applying a thin oxide-based surface coating can improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr.
The coating intervention is applicable from 500 to 1000 °C.
The coating intervention is applicable during exposure to air.
The coating intervention remains effective for exposures of up to 100 hours.
The coating intervention remains effective under tensile loading.
Application of the coating produces a stable oxide layer on the alloy surface.
The stable surface oxide layer acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
Blocking oxygen diffusion reduces the oxidation rate of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxide-based coatings are generally known to protect materials against oxidation in high-temperature environments.
Relative to untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, the coated alloy will have improved oxygen resistance.
Relative to untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, the coated alloy will have a lower oxidation rate.
The coating will increase the alloy's lifetime in high-temperature applications.
A coated specimen is expected to show a significant tensile-strength improvement over an uncoated specimen after the specified exposure.

contradictions.description: The central hypothesis requires improved oxygen resistance, but the falsification rule also treats lack of tensile-strength improvement as falsifying. Thus, a coating that clearly improves oxidation resistance while merely preserving rather than increasing tensile strength could be declared falsified even though it satisfies the stated hypothesis.
